title: catalog entry
description: One mod. The category decides which shape of `replaces` is legal, and the schema enforces it -- a Costume that omits `targets` does not validate, full stop. That is the difference between this and the old checker, which could only ask whether a sentence looked about right.

id.description: author.slug, lowercase. The install directory and the registry key.

credits.description: Who made it and how it reached us. Every entry owes this -- it is the debt we can always pay, even when the source URL is a dead forum.

replaces.description: The rendered sentence, GENERATED from replaces_data. Never hand-written -- CI asserts it equals render_replaces.render(replaces_data). Kept as a plain string so launcher builds older than v0.2.126, which type this field as String, keep working.

allOf.description:
Wearables owe item ids WHEN an item exists -- and `objects` when one does not. The first draft of this rule demanded `targets` outright, on the belief that there is always an item behind a costume, a mount or a weapon skin. 34 entries proved otherwise: the fishing float is a single global mesh in FishingResourceData that nothing equips, an NPC recolor targets a townsperson nobody can wear, and armour mesh packages are not named anywhere in the datacenter (poporiFemalePartid spans 0-510325104 with no positional encoding, so `Popori_F_H31` cannot be joined to an item by name).

Demanding an id that does not exist does not raise the bar, it forces a fabricated one -- and a fabricated target is exactly what made a costume mod import ballast over an outfit it never touched, twice. `objects` is the stricter answer, not the softer one: it is read out of the payload and re-verified against it.
Customization has no item at all -- it owes the character-creator slot and race. Some `Hair` entries are hair ACCESSORIES with real items, so either shape passes here.
Interface and system mods owe a named surface, and must NOT claim item ids they cannot have.
A gpk entry must say WHAT it swaps. External tools (Shinra, TCC) are overlay apps that swap no game asset, so `replaces` has nothing true to say and its absence is the honest answer.

A gpk entry must say HOW it deploys. Multi-part entries carry a strategy per part instead of one at the top level -- either is fine, neither is not: without one it installs, reports success, and does nothing.
